utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Today we are to have the closing arguments in this case, and we begin with the Prosecution. Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon, Mr. Tapuskovic, Ms. Isailovic. Today the Prosecution presents its oral closing submission to you. I will start off with a few introductory comments. My colleagues John Docherty and Manoj Sachdeva will then address the sniping and shelling parts of the evidence. Ms. Edgerton will then go into the terror campaign, and we will conclude -- and I will conclude with aspects of the criminal responsibility of the accused and sentencing submissions. I hope that we will stay within the two hours allocated to the Prosecution. Of course we have filed a week ago our comprehensive written brief, and to the extent possible we will try not to repeat ourselves today. My three colleagues and I will also respond to any relevant issue raised in the Defence brief. Your Honours, when Martin Bell the renowned BBC journalist testified before you, he commented his BBC footage of the aftermath of the Markale II massacre that occurred on 28 August 1995 with these words: "I think it's one of the most shocking of the war. On many occasions, and that was one of them, I was thinking to myself that if you ever tried to make a movie of this war, you couldn't. The scenes going on around me could not be replicated for a movie. They were so terrible, and they were real world and really shocking. And I also felt this cannot go on. We were more than three years into it, and I said to myself, You know, this cannot go on. It has to be stopped in the name of our common humanity. That's what I thought." Martin Bell at page 5.266. Your Honours, Markale II was one of the last and one of the most serious of the uncountable incidents that terrorised the civilians living inside the city of Sarajevo since the siege began in April 1992. You have heard the testimony of many witnesses, internationals, military observers, journalists, locals, who told you what life was like inside the confrontation lines. You will also recall the contemporaneous videos of news reports, the pictures, the daily, weekly UN situation reports. My colleagues will remind you in their presentations of some of these testimonies and other pieces of evidence, all proof of the daily suffering of the civilian population inside the confrontation lines during the siege. Even the most prominent, I guess, Defence witness Colonel Demurenko described how the civilians were worn out, appeared to be lethargic after the long siege. And he was talking about 1995. He added in response to a question by Judge Harhoff that: "If one looks at the human suffering, then it was a case of a full siege just like in Leningrad during the Second World War." Your Honours, the campaign that terrorised Sarajevo did not just start from August 1994 when the accused took command over from General Galic as the commander of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps, the SRK, the corps responsible for maintaining the siege of the city of Sarajevo. The history of what occurred before August 1994 was addressed extensively in the trial and Appeals Chamber judgements in the Prosecution of General Galic, and also by numerous witnesses during this trial against this accused, Dragomir Milosevic. Of relevance to this case is that there can be no question that before August 1994 the SRK subjected Sarajevo to a prolonged and murderous campaign of terror through shelling and sniping of civilians. During much of this earlier part of the campaign, the accused Dragomir Milosevic held prominent positions in the SRK. The campaign, as I mentioned, started in April and May 1992. I will only refer to two pieces of evidence that relate to that early part of the siege. First, the statement by the minister of health of the then-Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina as quoted in Prosecution Exhibits 462, pages 25 and 26. The minister of health who advocated destroying one of Sarajevo's major medical facilities, the Kosevo Hospital so that the enemy has nowhere to go for medical help. And second, P815, in which then-President Slobodan Milosevic is telling French UNPROFOR General Morillon that the bombardment of Sarajevo by Ratko Mladic was bloody, criminal, and that there was no justification for the continued bombardment of the civilian population of Sarajevo. This bloody and criminal campaign continued for 44 months. Your Honours, you heard live testimony about this campaign as it developed. According to witnesses before you who were able to compare the first part of the siege with the situation under the regime of this accused, it was for 44 months the same relentless campaign. The same characteristics, the same dynamics, the same weapons, front lines, soldiers, defenders, the same suffering of the civilians inside the confrontation lines, the same senseless punishing of the civilian population of Sarajevo for what happened elsewhere in Bosnia. In fact, there is evidence, like the introduction of the modified air bombs, that it got even worse. My colleagues will talk in more detail about all aspects of the campaign led by the accused. Let me address a few issues the Defence has raised in the course of the trial and also in their closing brief. Any Defence argument that the reason civilians were killed and injured was due to the deliberate intermingling by the ABiH of military targets with civilians and civilian objects is an attempt to draw attention away from the charges at hand. If the Defence is saying that the accused had information that civilians were mixed among military targets, the accused was under an obligation to gather sufficient information to ensure that any attacks against such a target, the anticipated military advantage outweighed the anticipated loss to civilian life. While civilian objects like schools and apartments, if indeed used for military purposes, can indeed become legitimate military objects for the time they are so used, there must be some evidence actually supporting this claim and not mere speculation. Second and most importantly, even if certain civilian objects become legitimate objects of attack, any such attack must still be conducted with respect for the principles of distinction and proportionality. It does not carte blanche authorise indiscriminate attacks or attacks causing excessive collateral damage. The trial record shows that not only did the accused make no effort to diminish the impact of the attacks on the civilian population, the SRK did not primarily shell and snipe at military targets. On the contrary, the evidence shows that the SRK, under command of the accused, fired directly at any locations where they knew civilian casualties would result intentionally and systematically. In fact they used air bombs to maximise the damage to civilian lives. This case is not about violations of international humanitarian law committed by the ABiH, the Bosnian Muslim army. It is about the individual criminal responsibility of this accused. Nor is it the case about the suffering which normally accompanies life during an armed conflict. This is a case about the direct intentional, unlawful targeting of civilians as a systematic strategy of the SRK under the command of the accused. The evidence in this case is also not about civilians being killed by accident in crossfire between the warring factions. Civilian witnesses who gave evidence of the direct targeting of themselves, their families, and their communities, did not testify to armed combat operations in the vicinity, to fighting breaking out near them, or to living in fear of a battle occurring in their neighbourhoods. Instead, they testified to being targeted at purely civilian locations, engaging in purely civilian activities, and to living in sheer terror that they would be intentionally targeted whilst engaging in a daily effort to survive. On 8 July 1995, to look at this issue from the UN perspective, the UNPROFOR weekly situation report prepared by David Harland stated: "Sniping and mortaring are still at a reasonably high level. This seems to have no particular military value but contributes to a general atmosphere of terror in the city." Prosecution Exhibit 20, page 2. The evidence shows that the accused and the SRK whom he commanded appear to have a policy of not aiming at military targets but targeting civilians instead. Witness Fraser testified that neither corps headquarters was attacked. Page 1796. Fraser added: "Indirect fire from the Muslims was replied by indirect fire from the Serbians, but it was a lot more and not directed to the headquarters. It was just directed to the city." Page 1801. Actions of the Bosnian Muslim army, as I said, in this regard are not relevant to the issue at hand. The amended indictment charges the accused with violations of the Laws and Customs of War, crimes against humanity. Indirect fire from the ABiH does not justify the intentional and unlawful targeting of civilians even where the motive is or might be response or retaliation. Regardless of the motive, if the primary purpose of the attacks was to spread terror, the means and methods are contrary to the international law and the accused bears individual criminal responsibility. As David Harland testified, page 324 and 25, "Most," and I quote: "Most of the military activity that I was reporting on was not military activity as you would conventionally understand it. Most of it was undirected or semi-directed artillery fire against civilian inhabited areas." And David Harland was the longest serving UN official in Sarajevo with vast amount of experience. You saw him as the first Prosecution witness. Your Honours, the civilians in Sarajevo suffered directly from the criminal means and methods used by the SRK under the accused. The SRK was not fighting a conventional war between two military forces. They were carrying out a terror campaign against Sarajevo's civilian population. Let me come to a second issue. On many occasions, and again in their closing brief, the Defence tries to advance the theory that nothing happened during the indictment before the start of the ABiH attempt to break out of the city in June 1995 when the situation of the encircled population became truly desperate. Evidence in this trial shows a completely different picture. I would like to refer you to only a few examples mainly based on UN reports, Prosecution Exhibit 10, 12, 15, also the evidence provided by General Smith gives a very good account of what happened. Let me start in late 1994. P10, of 10 December 1994, states that the Serbs made UNPROFOR's task almost impossible: "Having pushed UNPROFOR to brink of withdrawal, e.g., for instance by not allowing any humanitarian convoys into the city, allowing almost no gas into the city and with Serbs firing small guided missiles and anti-tank rockets into the downtown area causing a number of civilian casualties." Page 6 of Prosecution Exhibit 10. Next Prosecution Exhibit 12, a UN report in mid-April 1995 shows that the military situation in the city remained tense and mortar shells fell in the populated areas of the city causing deaths and casualties, and the fuel situation was so bad that UNPROFOR operations were seriously affected. The airport of Sarajevo was closed and eight international non-military hostages such as NGO workers were held by the Serbs. Prosecution Exhibit P12, page 1. Also in April, Your Honours, we of course have the first launchings of air bombs in the -- into Sarajevo. Prosecution Exhibit 703. In fact, in April 1995, the situation was so bad for the civilians that the Bosnian Ministry of Interior made the decision to forbid the gathering of people in public places in order to avoid large-scale incidents. Page 2 of Prosecution Exhibit 12. In early June 1995, Your Honours, the food situation in the city was rapidly deteriorating. Prosecution Exhibit 15, page 3. And this was due to the fact that the UNHCR land convoys could no longer operate. And in the same exhibit, Radovan Karadzic declared all UN Resolutions that applied to Sarajevo null and void. Prosecution Exhibit 15, page 3.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could you slow down a little, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You heard that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Yes. The trial record is replete, Your Honours, with evidence of the suffering of the civilian population inside Sarajevo during a time the Defence considers to be a lull. Led me address lastly before I turn over to my colleague Mr. Docherty the role of the several schedule incidents and our evidence in general. Another Defence argument was that the indictment or the allegations of a campaign are supported only by the selected incidents listed in the indictment. That, of course, is not the case. As is explicitly stated in the indictment and has always been our position, the scheduled incidents are illustrative and of course upon the orders, Mr. President, Your Honours, we had to reduce them by roughly one-third. There is, however, other additional significant and necessary evidence to prove the campaign. In other words, the evidence of the campaign of shelling and sniping and of terror is supported by the scheduled incidents, by evidence of unscheduled incidents and by other general evidence of witnesses and documents showing that throughout the indictment period there existed a campaign of shelling and sniping of civilian objects. It is critical that the proof of the campaign depends on different types of evidence of the sort I just mentioned, not simply the scheduled incidents. My colleagues will address this in more detail with relation to shelling and sniping. Let me now hand over to Mr. Docherty.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. President. Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon, Counsel. The Prosecution has proven the existence of a campaign against civilians that was conducted by the SRK under the accused's command and during the indictment period. One component of this campaign was the deliberate sniping of civilians. The evidence proving this is set out in detail in the Prosecution's closing brief, and I shall not repeat here material that is set out in that brief but shall only briefly summarise it. The accused ordered, planned, and/or aided and abetted this sniping campaign. He is therefore criminally liable for counts 2, 3, and 4 of the amended indictment under Article 7(1) of this Tribunal's Statute. More than that, the accused failed to take any measures to either prevent this illegal sniping campaign or to punish its perpetrators even though those perpetrators were troops over whom he had effective control and the accused knew that they were carrying out a campaign of terror. He is therefore criminally liable also, or in the alternative under Article 7(3) of the Tribunal's Statute for the sniping campaign. The relevant sections of the Prosecution's closing brief to which I respectfully refer the Chamber for a full discussion of the evidence demonstrating the existence of a sniping campaign include the campaign section itself at pages 5 through 9, the introduction to sniping at pages 15 to 18, and of course the scheduled and the unscheduled sniping incidents that are found throughout the discussion of incidents. Those incidents are organised by area, not by type of incident, and that is found at pages 18 to 98. I intend to give a very brief overview of the sniping campaign evidence but again repeat that the best and most thorough evidence is found in the Prosecution's closing brief. I shall then respond to some of the Defence criticisms of that evidence and during my time hope to discuss three other matters: Defence criticisms of the report of our expert demographer Ewa Tabeau; the issue of the control of the high ground; and the claimed, but as we shall see baseless, defence of alibi. Vekaz Turkovic, a crime scene technician with the Sarajevo police stated during the war calls for help on sniping and shelling came in from all other the city at all hours of the day and night at all times of the year, and that he and his colleagues in law enforcement spent 80 per cent of their time responding to these calls and working on these cases. When the war ended, these calls dropped to zero. A spreadsheet of police activity P602 was introduced. Now, of course this spreadsheet cannot be used as evidence of origin of fire, but there is a mass of other evidence in the discussions of the individual incidents indicating uniformly that the origin of fire was SRK territory, and contrary to the Defence assertions made at paragraphs 143 to 146 of their closing brief, this spreadsheet is perfectly good evidence of the intensity of the nature, of the number of incidents. And when coupled with the origin of fire evidence that was independently introduced, it is powerful evidence of the existence of a campaign.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Docherty, you place obviously a lot of emphasis on this campaign, the proof of a campaign. Suppose you don't prove the existence of a campaign. Does your case fail?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: No, Mr. President, it certainly does not. The allegations in the amended indictment charge the accused with crimes against humanity and with murder and with inhumane acts. The existence of a campaign has relevance to the terror count and because crimes against humanity require a -- that the individual attack be part of a pattern it has some relevance to the crimes against humanity, but I would put it that a campaign, that in fact all of the charges in the indictment can be proven in the absence of or if there is reasonable doubt about the existence of a campaign. However, I should hope that there would not be at the end of the day reasonable doubt about the existence of a campaign. The evidence concerning that being in my view so very strong and consisting of the scheduled incidents, the unscheduled incidents, and then what I call the overview evidence from witnesses such as Martin Bell, Mr. Turkovic, the various internationals who came here and gave evidence before you, all of whom spoke of the intensity, of the duration, of the thoroughgoing nature of the SRK's attacks on the civilian population.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I raise the question because it is almost as though you have made the campaign an element of the crime, of crimes against humanity and the crime of terror when it is not. What you have to prove are the ingredients required for a crime against humanity, and those are well known, and the ingredients for the crime of terror, perhaps not as well known as the first. And so it has always struck me, I've always wondered why the Prosecution has set itself this task as though it has transformed the campaign into a legal requirement for the -- for proof of the crimes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: I am sorry if we have given that impression, Mr. President, and two things. First of all, my colleague Ms. Edgerton will speak specifically to the terror count. But second of all, the evidence in this case does show the existence of a campaign, and since the evidence shows the existence of a campaign and shows that a campaign was what the SRK was about for the 15 months of this indictment period, by showing this campaign we necessarily show the broad pattern of attacks necessary for a crime against humanity, and we also, of course, show the individual inhumane acts, but, you know, the SRK, its officers and its men, didn't have the elements of crimes against humanity in mind as they went about their daily business around Sarajevo. They had a campaign to conduct, and therefore by illustrating that campaign we show that that campaign necessarily proves crimes against humanity and inhumane acts and -- or indeed all of the crimes alleged in the indictment. So it is meant to be the best, the most thorough, the most accurate description of the reality of what the SRK was about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. I think you have put it very well there. I see it as merely descriptive, illustrative of the Prosecution's case.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: It's not a legal requirement. It's not an ingredient.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: It is not an ingredient. It is not an element. It is a description of what was really happening, and of course by describing what was really happening we are legally describing crimes against humanity and inhumane acts and so on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: It's as though -- I'm trying to think of a parallel. If a man is charged with -- with raping, say, in domestic jurisdiction, and it is said that he's a serial rapist but he's charged with raping one particular individual, the Prosecution's case is that this man is a serial rapist. He has raped perhaps 12 or 20 women, and that is described in the Prosecution's case. But if the Prosecution fails to prove the seriality of the offence, it hasn't failed if it nonetheless proves he has raped the particular person charged in the indictment.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Saying that he's a serial rapist is nearly a way of describing and illustrating the Prosecution's case. And when I read your brief as well as the case that has preceded this one, I wonder if the -- the two have not been confused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Because so much -- so much time is spent on trying to prove this campaign. Of course it may well be that if you prove it you prove your case.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: That is my belief, Mr. President, that if we prove it, we have proven our case. And if I may respond to your analogy with one of my own. It's usually in domestic prosecutions the motive for a crime is not an element of a crime. Nevertheless, describing the motive is a great assistance in capturing the crime and in showing the pattern into which the crime fits. And here the campaign is what the SRK was doing, crimes against humanity, inhumane acts are the legal categories into which that behaviour fits.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: And that is what you are required to prove. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Further evidence generally of the intensity of the sniping against civilian targets and of the exclusively civilian nature of those targets is found in one of the Prosecution's first witnesses, Thorbjorn Overgard, a UNMO from Norway, who was stationed in Hrasnica, who investigated sniping incidents in Hrasnica almost every day and who testified at pages 636 that the origin of fire was always SRK territory and the victim was always a civilian. He never investigated a single case in which a soldier had been shot. There is evidence in this case that the SRK had the means to snipe on civilians. Silencers, telescopic sites, requisitions for sniping ammunition --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Please slow down for the interpreters, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And I refer to Exhibit P664, P765, 766, and 767. Dr. Tabeau testified that even on militarily quiet days civilians continued to be killed in violent, war-related ways mostly as a result of sniping. Speaking of Ms. Tabeau, I divert for a moment or two because at paragraph 139 and following of the Defence brief there are some criticisms of her work which in my view and the Prosecution's view are unfounded. Paragraph 139, the Defence asserts that Ms. Tabeau only gives casualty figures for within the confrontation lines. The accused on trial here is, of course -- was, of course, the commander of the SRK, and therefore of course the analysis will focus on his alleged victims and they will be found inside the confrontation lines. At paragraph 140 the Defence claims that Ms. Tabeau mixed up the indictment period with the total time of the conflict. In fact, when she testified at page 5549, she made clear that she used the total conflict time only by means of -- for means of context. I also would refer the Tribunal in terms of unscheduled sniping incidents particularly to Prosecution Exhibits 92 and 95. Both of those are the 92 ter evidence of victims of scheduled incidents who also testified that they themselves had not only been victims or had known a victim of a scheduled incident but also of an unscheduled incident, which is evidence of the thoroughgoing nature of this activity that it could strike multiple citizens of Sarajevo multiple times. Police officer Nedzib Djozo testified that every day there was sniping from Spicasta Stijena and that many civilians were killed or wounded as a result. Speaking of Sharpstone, the evidence is clear, the Defence contention to the contrary, notwithstanding that the SRK controlled Sharpstone throughout the indictment period. The Defence in paragraph 184 of their brief says that Sedrenik was a military zone throughout the conflict but when one looks for a citation or a footnote of authority one finds none. There is a claim that the local inhabitants never referred to it by that name and a claim that in fact it did not overlook Sedrenik but Grdonj the citation is to page 7059 but when one looks at that one finds only the unremarkable and uncontroversial assertion that Sharpstone and Grdonj and Hum are all part of the same geological feature. But it is when we come to the question of where the confrontation lines are that the Defence submissions become truly confused, and on this I would invite the Chamber to compare Exhibits D256 and D257. These are the same photograph. Two different Defence witnesses were asked to draw the confrontation lines on those photographs. They vary considerably. Against this, the Prosecution has presented clear evidence from local inhabitants, United Nations military officers, law enforcement officers, and even from Defence witnesses that Sharpstone was under the control of the SRK and that therefore sniping from Sharpstone is sniping that came from the SRK. Any claim that sniping from Sharpstone came from the ABiH is unfounded. As police officer Nedzib Djozo testified, Sedrenik where the victims where was not even visible from the ABiH positions which were at the bottom and two the side of the Sharpstone feature. T3689. And finally there is one set of facts that I don't believe the Defence has even tried to refute, which is that even if an ABiH soldier could see Sharpstone, and the evidence is that this soldier could -- see Sedrenik, and the evidence is this soldier could not, any ABiH soldier who actually took such a shot would be taking his life in his hands as he would have to stand up and turn his back on the enemy to fire into Sedrenik. And even over and above that, this hypothetical soldier would have been firing at his own friends and family since the ABiH soldiers in that area were locally recruited. T3690. A number of the Prosecution's scheduled incidents concern firing upon trams. In each and every case, every witness to these incidents testified unequivocally that there were no ABiH military personnel or equipment in the area and that there was no combat going on. Despite this unanimity of evidence, the Defence asserts in paragraph 88 that it was irresponsible of the Bosnian government to allow trams to run near the front lines. The claim seems to be that that made them vulnerable to being caught in a crossfire, to which the most readily available, most obvious response is: What crossfire, when witnesses have said that there was no combat going on? The closest the Defence ever came to making out a claim of crossfire, and it really was not close at all, was a claim respect to sniping incident 13 on 27 February, 1995, that a firefight was going on at the Vrbanja bridge at the same time that a tram was sniped. And if we could please see Prosecution Exhibit 182 on the screen. While that's coming up, General Fraser was cross-examined about this. The UN report was given to him. He testified at page 1887 that he read this report to be about two separate incidents with the tram sniping completely separate from the firefight at the bridge. But this Defence claim of crossfire was definitively shot down by witness Alma Cehajic Mulaosmanovic who testified that the bridge and tram were outside of each other and marked a photograph on the screen in front you to make this plain. On this photograph, Your Honours, the blue marks on the right are the bridge. The two parallel lines immediately south of the Tito barracks are the area where the sniping occurred, and the red circle is the witness's evidence as to the origin of fire. One can see here that sniping incident 13 was in no way the result of a tram being caught in a crossfire. The Defence also claimed that paragraph 4 of Prosecution Exhibit 175 is evidence that soldiers and civilians were mixed up on these trams. When one goes and checks the reference, one sees that a single soldier was on a tram. Whether he was in or out of uniform is not known, and in light of what happened next, not important, because that tram, the witness goes on to say, was shot with 30 machine-gun bullets in and just under the windows of the tram. And finally the Defence claimed that the Bosnian government, by running the trams, was putting civilians in harm's way is simply unfounded. The Defence does not mention in its brief that the trams only ran during cease-fires and that therefore each and every one of the four tram sniping incidents about which the Prosecution led evidence is a cease-fire violation. The Defence also makes the claim that the S curve about what we heard so much evidence in front of the Holiday Inn was not visible from the Metalka building overlooking the fact that it is visible from elsewhere in Grbavica and also overlooking, of course, that trams slow down before they enter the curve and speed up slowly as they are leaving the curve so that their total vulnerable time is much greater than simply the time that they spend in the S curve. Mr. President and Your Honours, I want to spend just a couple of minutes now talking about the defence of alibi and the issue of who controlled the high ground. The Prosecution has put forth a good deal of evidence in its closing brief concerning the accused's effective control over the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps. The only real challenge, I submit, to this evidence has been a claim that the accused is not liable for the Markale massacre of 28 August 1995, because on that day he was in the hospital in Belgrade having an eye injury attended to. As we say in our brief, the fact that the terror campaign continued in the accused's absence is actually incriminating. It shows that the machinery which the accused had set in motion could continue even in his absence. It is also worth drawing the Chamber's attention, and I respectfully do draw your attention, to the testimony of Defence witness Veljovic who testified at pages 5844 and 45 that the accused, of course, would have been briefed about events upon his return from Belgrade and yet despite this there is no evidence whatsoever that the accused ever prosecuted anyone or disciplined anyone for the dreadful crime that was committed on August 28th. On the issue of who controlled the high ground around Sarajevo. Let me start this discussion again with something I've been talking about for a couple of minutes, which is Grbavica. In paragraph 41 of their brief, the Defence concedes that Grbavica was controlled by the SRK. It was hemmed in on three sides by the ABiH and on the fourth side was the front line, the Miljacka river. The Defence then goes on to claim, however, that this does not matter in that Grbavica is dominated by Debelo Brdo. They give a transcript cite for this proposition, and unfortunately when one checks the source one finds that it flatly contradicts the Defence assertion. It is a citation to the testimony of General Fraser, and in it he first agrees with counsel that there is a pretty good view of Sniper Alley from Debelo Brdo, adds, but it's a long way away though. And in any event, the SRK, as General Fraser testified, looked down on Debelo Brdo. Transcript 1768. It is also worth -- or I point out that line of sight is important for direct-fire weapons such as rifles. It is not important for indirect-fire weapons such as mortars, and that the only scheduled incidents that we refer to that we claim came from a hilltop are those that came from Sharpstone. But over and above Debelo Brdo, there is significant evidence that it was the SRK that controlled the higher points all the way around Sarajevo. In the south-east, Trebevic, in the north-east Sharpstone, Mrkovici, and Poljane and it is from these that the city was bombarded.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Docherty, I want to go back to the issue of what you call the Defence argument about an alibi, although it doesn't appear to me to be -- to be a question of alibi at all. When the accused went to the hospital to have his eye treated, at that time the evidence is, if my recollection is correct, that the authority and control had been transferred to his deputy, so that he was not in de jure control of the operations. So I don't see this really as raising a question of alibi. It is simply that he lacked the de jure authority. De facto may be another matter, but he lacked the authority at that time. And how does it answer that argument for you to say that the machinery that he had set up was so well-oiled that it continued to function efficiently in his absence?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: My recollection, Mr. President, was that the Defence put into evidence a number of medical records without our objection because indeed we do not contest that he was absent from the theatre at this time, but it is also worth pointing out that he returned from -- from Belgrade, that he would have been, according to Mr. Veljovic, fully briefed, that he took no action. So there are two things going on. Number one, the accused has set up, has administered over a period of months this, without opening that whole can of worms, campaign. That campaign continues to run --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What about 7(3).

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: 7(3), Your Honour, to paraphrase, says that if you have effective control over troops and you know they are committing crimes and you fail to take the reasonable and necessary steps that you can take - the impossible is not required - reasonable and necessary steps then you are guilty of the crimes committed by those troops.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: And you were submission is that notwithstanding that he was in the hospital having his eye tended to and even more significantly, in his absence the authority over the troops had been transferred to somebody else that he nonetheless had effective control?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: No. Well, it's that argument but that's an alternative argument. The primary argument of course is that he ordered and he planned the campaign, and this is where the campaign does come in. He ordered and planned a campaign of terror against the civilian population. The fact that I plan to rob a bank next week and that my confederates go ahead and rob the bank next week but that I leave town does not absolve me of criminal liability for ordering and planning that bank robbery any more than it should absolve the accused of criminal liability for ordering, and planning, and aiding and abetting the campaign of terror against the civilians of Sarajevo during the indictment period.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Very well. We'll hear the Defence on that point.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Just briefly to finish up the issue of control of the high ground. To take two examples, Zuc and Hum. The Defence argues and they are correct that the ABiH had control of these features, but they overlook the fact these features are themselves surrounded, overlooked, controlled by far higher summits, and Trebevic, if we look at the map D59, which was the map that hung in the courtroom for, I believe, days on end, Trebevic is above a thousand metres. In the south Grad and Faletici are in the 850 to 1.000 metre heights range. Poljine in the north and Paljevo in the west are both 900 to a thousand metres. All of these surrounding hills are littered with the sort of heavy weaponry that could be used and was used to pound Sarajevo day after day during the indictment period.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What's the -- the legal significance of holding the high ground?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: There is factual significance in holding the high ground in that -- well, there are two -- two issues here. First of all, with respect to indirect fire weapons like mortars, it is -- it does not matter who holds the high ground. What matters is that the mortars are fired from outside the city into the city. For direct fire weapons it does matter. Direct fire weapons one does need to see the target, but again, I do think that the question of control of the high ground, a fair amount of time was spent on it, perhaps not entirely necessarily since, as I say, the control of the high ground for direct fire weapons that we allege is important is the control of the Sharpstone feature which I think when one examines all of the evidence is clearly -- was controlled by the SRK. So there is also, of course, in the introductory matters in the in the indictment, in the amended indictment, a reference to the SRK controlling high ground around Sarajevo. So I would put it, however, that although the ABiH did hold a hill here and a hill there, all of these are the Debelo Brdo situation, which is the ABiH does hold an elevation, but they do not hold the best real estate in that particular area because the SRK holds even higher ground that looks down upon the ABiH feature, and that the overall picture painted at the beginning of the -- of the amended indictment, which is that Sarajevo lies in a valley and that it is dominated by the hills that surround that valley and that those hills were dominated by the SRK is correct, notwithstanding that the ABiH did, of course, hold an elevation here and an elevation there. The overall pattern is that the SRK held the high ground looking down into the valley of the Miljacka river, looking down into the city of Sarajevo. Mr. President, Your Honours, in a couple of places the Defence has made assertions in its brief that really are not supported by the evidence at all. In particular, I want to draw the Chamber's attention to paragraphs 150 and 151 of the Defence's closing brief. In those paragraphs, the Defence asserts first that UNPROFOR and the UNMOs had difficulty counting the number of wounded because they were not always allowed access to Sarajevo hospitals, and then go on in paragraph 151 to say that in any event, the numbers of wounded were inflated because wounded were brought in from outside Sarajevo through the tunnel and put in hospitals around town. That's paragraph 151. There is a cite. It is to the testimony of General Karavelic. He does say that the wounded were transported in the tunnel. To take that citation to General Karavelic and to turn it on its head, I mean obviously General Karavelic is talking about evacuating wounded from the city. And to make the completely unfounded claim that the Bosnian authorities were inflating the numbers of wounded by bringing civilians in wounded from elsewhere in Bosnia and planting them in hospitals that then couldn't even be counted because the Defence also claims that the United Nations couldn't get into the hospital, is an argument that really should not delay the Chamber for very long. The same might be said of some of the allegations that the Defence has made concerning the quality of the police work done by Bosnian law enforcement. For example, at paragraph 153, the very serious allegation of tampering with a crime scene is made, but it turns out that if anything happened what happened is that the scene was washed. This has not the slightest effect, as witnesses testified, on the shape, the depth, or the position of a crater. It also has no effect on statements of witnesses. The Defence seeks to make much of the absence of investigating judges, and yet, investigating judges, it appears, did not always go along with the police.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Is there evidence that washing the scene had no effect on the -- what is it you say?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: The shape of a crater. The size of a crater, the depth of a crater.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You have adduced evidence to that effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. We have adduced evidence to that effect. From more than one witness. If you wash off the crater and get the grisly remains of one of these incidents away,, the crater is still there and the crater canter analysis is what matters here. Similarly no prejudice can be shown from the absence of an investigating judge. Nothing can be pointed out that the police did or did not do that would have been different had the investigating judge been there. The claim is made that photographs were not taken of victims in situ, but of course once a victim falls down, the victim's orientation as to the origin of fire also changes and therefore photographs of victims at the scene tell us nothing of forensic significance. The same is true of the Defence claim that biological samples were not taken. The absence of biological samples, the presence of biological samples for that matter, would help tell us absolutely nothing concerning the origin of fire. In conclusion, there was sniping systematically directed at the civilians of Sarajevo. The accused controlled that sniping. General Fraser said that if approached about sniping, if the accused was approached about sniping, things would get better for a while and then they would go downhill again. The anti-sniping agreement falls squarely into that pattern. Things got better for a while and then went downhill. But by signing that agreement the accused made it crystal clear that he controlled the activities of SRK snipers in Sarajevo, as do exhibits 765, 766, 767 in which the accused requisitions sniping ammunition for his troops. Patrick van der Weijden of the Dutch army, a sniping expert and experienced sniper himself with military experience in Bosnia, a trainer for the Dutch army of other snipers says that he visited the scene of every single scheduled sniping incident and in every single case fire should have been withheld because the shooter could not have identified the victim positively as a combatant. The Prosecution has proved its sniping case. Thank you, Mr. President, and thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Sachdeva.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. President, Your Honours, and good afternoon to the Defence. Mr. President, Your Honours, the Prosecution submits that it has proven beyond a reasonable doubt that the three mortar incidents, the one cannon and 11 modified air bomb incidents listed in schedule 2 of the amended indictment were committed by the accused and his SRK forces, thereby proving counts 1, 5, 6 and 7 of the amended indictment. I want to indicate at the outset that in the limited time that I have I don't intend to repeat the Prosecution's closing submissions regarding the shelling component of the amended indictment which can be found within pages 9 to 95 of the said brief. Rather, I will focus on two scheduled shelling incidents contained in schedule 2, where necessary respond to some of the Defence assertions made on them, and make submissions generally on the subject of modified air bombs. Mr. President and Your Honours, in the beginning I wish to remind the Trial Chamber of the following significant pieces of evidence that must in the Prosecution's submission be borne in mind when determining the ultimate issue, that is, the origin of fire, and this is quite apart from the scientific evidence that I will deal with in a moment. The first is from Defence Witness Glavas. He was a soldier with the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps stationed on the front lines, and at T8748 he was asked this question: "So in fact what you're saying is since you were surrounded, it's logical to assume that when a shell lands in your area it comes from the people who are surrounding you; is that correct?" The answer was an emphatic "Yes." The second piece of significant evidence comes from General Rupert Smith. He was the UNPROFOR commander throughout most of 1995 and was stationed in Sarajevo. When asked about the origin of fire for the Markale incident, he said and I quote: "And finally, it is my experience of being in a siege that round that fall on the inside of a siege tend to come from outside the siege." And, Mr. President and Your Honours, this is the incident that I now turn to, the Markale massacre, scheduled shelling incident 23. The Markale market Massacre on the 28th of August, 1995, in which over 40 civilians died and over 70 were injured represented the climax of the accused's campaign of terror through shelling of civilians in Sarajevo. It was the second most notorious incident in this location, just as the first Markale marketplace massacre on the 5th of February 1994 also caused, by a single 120-millimetre mortar round, marked the tenure of General Galic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: On behalf of the interpreters may I ask you to slow down.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: I apologise to the interpreters. Just as the first marketplace massacre on the 5th of February, 1994, also caused by a single 120-millimetre mortar round, marked the tenure of General Galic, General Milosevic's predecessor, so the shelling on the 28th of August, 1995, marked the tenure of the accused. The Markale shelling attack symbolises the unnecessary suffering of the civilian population in Sarajevo during the accused's tenure as SRK commander. And, Mr. President, Your Honours, the Prosecution does call this a shelling because when one looks at the hard scientific facts on the trial record, this is exactly what it was, a single round of a 120-millimetre mortar grenade fired from SRK-controlled Mount Trebevic by an SRK mortar crew on a late summer morning, exploding at the marketplace in downtown Sarajevo, killing and maiming civilians. Mr. President, Your Honours, there are versions of events that are quite -- that are supported by evidence and there are versions that are not. Quite simply, only the Prosecution's version of events is supported and corroborated by the evidence you have heard in this trial. The Prosecution's account of the Markale massacre is a detailed reconstruction based upon a painstaking evaluation of the scientific evidence developed during four separate official contemporaneous investigations. Because the Prosecution's account is based on evidence, we are able to tell the Court that it has been established beyond a reasonable doubt that a 120-millimetre shell fired from SRK positions on Mount Trebevic, situated south of the explosion site, flew along an approximate 170-degree direction, entered the busy market at an angle of no shallower than 67 degrees, hit a point in the main road roughly 4.8 metres from the wall of the south-facing building and exploded, causing the human destruction that is graphically depicted in video P623 and P355. The evidence of civilian casualties is also recorded in medical records and autopsy reports and they are P71 through to P82. And significantly the evidence of casualties is witnessed firsthand by victims of the shelling themselves such as witness Mesuda Klaric in P648. The detailed analysis of the technical evidence is contained in paras 302 to 338 of the Prosecution's final brief. Suffice it to say that the first UN investigation conducted by UNMO witness Konings who arrived at the scene 30 to 40 minutes after the explosion concluded that a 120-millimetre mortar round had exploded and this is contained in his report, P85. This was confirmed by a separate independent Bosnian investigation in Prosecution Exhibit 252, under seal, and a further UN report conducted by the French Engineering Cell at Prosecution Exhibit 357, page 6. The direction of fire of the shell, that is 170 degrees, plus minus the 10 degree margin of error is also not in doubt. Konings, the Bosnian MUP investigation, and the French investigation all concluded the approximate direction of fire to be near the 170 degree mark. Expert witness Higgs, who as the Trial Chamber recalls testified as an expert in the Galic case and whose whole career had been devoted to mortars and who was the most senior officer in the British Army regarding mortars, confirmed that the 120-millimetre explosion had occurred after examining photographs of the crater. Even Defence expert witness Garovic said that the correction was 175 degrees and I refer Your Honours to paragraph 313 to 318 of the brief. It is clear that the 120-millimetre shell flew in from south of the city in the direction of Mount Trebevic which was indisputably under SRK control. That the shell was fired across the confrontation lines, in other words, in SRK territory, and not from within the confrontation lines, that is within ABiH territory, has been shown beyond a reasonable doubt in large part by the evidence of Witness Thom Knustad. Knustad was a Norwegian UNMO with extensive experience in artillery. On the morning the 28th of August, 1995, he along with his colleagues Paul Conway were posted in a UN observation point called OP1, which was situated close to the confrontation lines to the south of the city towards Mount Trebevic and was roughly one kilometre away from the flight path of the shell. Now why is this important? It is important because Knustad and Conway were deployed at a location that if a 120-millimetre shell had been fired from within ABiH territory along this flight path then Knustad and Conway would have heard it. But the overwhelming evidence is that they did not hear the fire. And this means in the Prosecution's submission that the shell was not fired from ABiH lines. Knustad said it was possible to hear the sound of a 120-millimetre mortar being fired from some 4 to 5 kilometres away. Higgs confirmed that it could be heard from some 3 to 4 kilometres away and Defence expert Garovic corroborated this by saying it could be heard from some 5 to 6 kilometres away.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Kindly slow down for the interpreters, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: I apologise again. He also agreed that if an observer were one kilometre away from the firing position, he would have heard it. Knustad testified that he did not hear a mortar being fired from within the confrontation lines up until he saw the smoke-stack rising from the marketplace in town. He testified that if it had been fired from within the lines and in the direction of fire of 170 degrees, he would have heard it. The significance of this evidence is amplified by the UNMO team leader Konings. He was Knustad's team leader and he held Knustad in high professional regard, saying that he was an experienced military man with experience in artillery and mortars. Konings testified that OP1 reported to him that they did not hear any outgoing round. In answering a question as to the significance of the UNMOs at OP1 not hearing the round being fired, he said at T 3585 and I quote: "Well, it is a missing clue in trying to designate the origin of fire of that specific round. In case it would -- the round would have been fired from Bosnian territory, it would have been done -- in combination with this minimum angle of impact it would have been done with charge zero, the lowest charge you can fire. If you trace that back from the origin of impact you would have come in the area around OP1. The place of origin of fire would have been in the area around OP1. And since on that quiet day you cannot miss, to my professional opinion, an outgoing 120-millimetre round, it's a loud bang. You cannot miss it, you will see it, you will see the flash, you will see the smoke. Well, that brings you to the conclusion that the round came from further away. And since there was no noise heard, it must have come from behind the mountain ridge, which is on the south side of the city of Sarajevo, which muffles the sound." This evidence clearly establishes that the round was not fired by the ABiH but by the SRK as it must have been fired from a further distance away, beyond the confrontation lines and behind the mountain ridge. Knustad said it was very possible that the mortar was fired from behind the VRS line and that he would not have heard it because of the configuration of the terrain and the way the sound would move behind the hill, behind his position. Expert witness Higgs confirmed the neutralising effect on the sound by the hills. The Defence experts while agreeing that the sound would have been muffled maintain that the firing of the shell would have been heard by the UNMOs if it had been fired from VRS lines. Mr. President, the problem with this evidence is that not only is it contradicted by Higgs and by Konings and by Knustad, it is based upon the firing position being at 2.400 metres from the explosion site and does not take into account that the shell could have been fired from a further distance. It is correct that Higgs puts the likely firing position at 2.400 metres. But as the Prosecution has submitted during the trial and has indicated in our final trial brief at paragraph 312, the Prosecution's burden of proof is to establish that the round was fired within SRK territory and this is what has been established. But actually, Mr. President, Your Honours, the Defence haven't suggested this account at all. No. The Defence has maintained a radically different version of events and this is why at the beginning of my argument I stress the fact of a shelling incident, because quite to the contrary, the Defence assert that the destruction caused at the marketplace was the result of a static explosion, a terrorist attack caused in situ. Mr. President, Your Honours, in paragraphs 326 to 338 in its closing brief the Prosecution rebuts in detail the Defence theory of the explosion being the result of a static explosion and in the Prosecution's submission it is clear when one examines the evidence such a theory cannot be supported. The Defence argument on this issue is contained on page 66 of the English version of their brief. Firstly the Defence ask the Trial Chamber to rely on the expert report of Dr. Vukasinovic and that report is D175. This report concludes that the Markale shelling was the result of a static explosion. The Prosecution submits, however, that this report should not be afforded any weight by the Trial Chamber. Its author was not called by the Defence and his analysis and conclusions were not tested in cross-examination or by questions from the Bench and as such is unreliable. Initially, Dr. Vukasinovic relies on several assumptions. One example of this is his finding related to the angle of descent of the shell, noted on page 3 of the English version of his report. To determine the height of the south-facing building, a crucial measurement for the calculation of the angle of descent, Vukasinovic's determination of the height was based on an assumption of the average height of a person depicted in figure 4 and that assumption was that the man would have been 1.75 metres high. Now, Mr. President, this could be but it could also not be. If such an assumption is wrong then it throws the entire subsequent conclusions awry. The Defence in their brief state that Prosecution expert Zecevic agreed with the mathematics used by Vukasinovic and recognised his expertise in this field. Well, yes, this is correct in part. Zecevic accepted that the theory used by Dr. Vukasinovic was sound but he had serious concerns with the data the doctor used. This, the Defence did not reveal in their brief. Zecevic did not endorse a finding of a static explosion and I refer you, Mr. President and Your Honours, to transcripts page 4936 and 4937. Zecevic said the following: "In the study you mention there are several arguments that are misconceived. If we calculate the height of the building and the distance from the place of the incident we can determine that the angle of descent was at least 70 degrees whereas in Mr. Vukasinovic's study it says 50 to 60. It changes the whole thing and I underscore yet again, I want to stress that Mr. Vukasinovic is excellent in theory. However, in his study he used data that did not reflect the accurate situation."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Sachdeva, earlier you referred us to page 66 of the Defence brief, and I'm wondering whether that is the correct page.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: It's the English version, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, it's the last page, headed "Discussion."

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President, I apologise. I think it's page 57.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thanks.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: May I continue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, please. Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours. Good afternoon, Your Honours. I'm sorry to interrupt my learned friend, but I was expecting that we would receive the English translation if it's available. In the current situation, we are not able to follow properly. We did notice certain discrepancies, and I thought that if available we should have the English translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. I would think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President, perhaps I can assist my friend.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: It's also contained in pages -- paras 193 to 194 of the French original version of their brief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I'll ask the registrar to ensure that you receive a copy, Mr. Tapuskovic, of the English version. Are you sure you don't have it? We have had this experience before.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You certainly didn't have that experience with me, because I'm sure we didn't receive it, and we wanted to have it today before the closing arguments began. Right now we are not in a position to check the references my learned friend is making.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The paragraph numbers would be the same as in the French, but you are entitled, of course, to have the English version, and we'll see to that, Mr. Tapuskovic. Please continue, Mr. Sachdeva.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I had just - before this deviation - I had just finished quoting Dr. Zecevic, and I want to say that of course Dr. Vukasinovic made assumptions because he was not there, but the Bosnian and the UN investigators were there on the scene just after the explosion, and they arrived at specific calculations of the angle of descent, independent calculations and measurements which, Mr. President and Your Honours, in the Prosecution's submission are far more reliable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Sachdeva, I'm going to stop now to take the break. I understand, Mr. Tapuskovic, that you wish to make a submission, and I should say if a party wishes to make a submission it may do so. You don't need to have my permission. You just rise and make the submission.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, the only thing, Your Honours, that I wish to say, and I had indicated so before the beginning of this hearing, is that I could certainly start my own closing argument right away. Nevertheless, I wanted to say, and I am prompted by the problem with this translation additionally, and I am going to respect whatever the Chamber decides, but still I would like, after the closing argument of the Prosecution is finished, to have this document in order to prepare for tomorrow, in order to be as concise and as clear as possible in my response to the Prosecution, because I'm hardly in a position to respond to every argument made today. I see no reason for haste, and I still have time during the night and tomorrow morning to prepare properly. To that end, I wanted to say that I would appreciate it if you could enable me to do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We'll consider the submission. Of course the time available to you would still remain the same, two hours. Mr. Sachdeva.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President, I just would like to inform counsel that when I had referred to page 66, in fact it was of the French original version of the brief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Not the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Not the English version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thanks. Now, the Chamber will have to carry out some consultations in the break, and we will therefore break for a half an hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Sachdeva.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Before the break I had -- I was talking about Dr. Vukasinovic's report and as an aside, Mr. President, Your Honours, it is noted that the methodology used by Dr. Vukasinovic is the same as that used by the Bosnian investigators in arriving at specific calculations such as the angle of descent, and I make this point because the Defence, as my colleague Mr. Docherty has already told you, have in their brief questioned the competence and the qualifications of some of the Bosnian police. Now, the Defence have also said that their expert Garovic who was an experienced artillery officer also conclude that had it was a static explosion at the marketplace. Well, let's examine what this experienced artillery officer concluded. When confronted, he agreed that for there to have been a static explosion there would have been secondary marks on the ground from either the contraption that would have been used to hold the projectile in place or from the explosive device. He said he did not see evidence of secondary marks on the ground. Not unsurprisingly, expert witness Higgs corroborates this and he says at T5032: "Yes. If they had used a 120-millimetre bomb statistically, then it needed to be detonated in some way, either by placing a secondary charge on the side which would have affected the pattern tremendously." Now, as a response, Garovic appeared to suggest that there may have ban cover-up when the scene was cleaned but again when confronted he agreed that crater marks on the road would not have been altered by the cleaning of the crime site and, Mr. President, Your Honours, this fact is also corroborated by Witness 137, the Bosnian police investigator who was also at the scene after the explosion. The two experts Higgs and Garovic also agreed on another factor, that any static explosion would have had to have been detonated so as to coincide with the specific crater patterns found at the scene on the road. Higgs at 5031 said that with regard to the shrapnel patterns on the ground, if a round was put there statically, it would have to have been held in position by a frame to hold it at roughly 70 degrees to coincide with the crater marks. Defence expert Garovic agreed that the crater marks were not accidental but, rather, a result of a particular trajectory and angle of descent and therefore to produce a static explosion one would have to emulate these factors. UNMO witness Konings who testified that he had passed the marketplace some one or two hours before the explosion and said that he did not notice a crater, that to create a crater between the time he passed there and the time of the explosion would be, in his words, "impossible". The Defence also cite to Witness Demurenko's conclusion that it was a static explosion, specifically a terrorist attack. Mr. President and Your Honours, I don't want to repeat the Prosecution's detailed rebuttal of Demurenko's testimony, and I refer Your Honours to paragraphs 327 and 329 of the brief, but suffice it to say for this -- this argument, there are serious problems with his testimony and conclusions. Firstly, the data he used when coming to his conclusion that it was a static explosion was, in the Prosecution's submission, incorrect, and I refer Your Honours to his -- his figures of 120 people being killed. Secondly, he says that it was not possible to fire a single round at the same spot in two years, but this, Mr. President, disregards the evidence of Higgs and W-137 that it is possible to hit a target on the first shot when sites have been pre-recorded. And lastly, Demurenko himself admitted that he was not an anti-terrorist specialist, rather a peacekeeping specialist. Mr. President, Your Honours, when it boils down to it, you are being asked to believe that the Bosnian authorities conceived of a plan to create a contraption and explosive device that would be in range -- arranged in such a way so as to produce crater marks to reflect a 120-millimetre explosion and an angle of descent at roughly 70 degrees, that such a device would be wheeled in and set up amongst the throng of very people that the Bosnian authorities were defending while they were busy shopping and trading goods on a downtown street, without anyone noticing, and then detonating it. You are being asked to believe that the Bosnian authorities would sacrifice hundreds of their own people and that it could be done with such exposure without it coming to light in the past 12 years. This conspiratorial version, Mr. President and Your Honours, is completely unbelievable over the most obvious, logical and scientific one, and that is a 120-millimetre mortar was fired by the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps from Mount Trebevic exploding at the busy marketplace. The Prosecution submits that the evidence is beyond clear. This account is what happened on that fateful morning of the 28th of August, 1995, and the static explosion theory is basically what Defence expert Garovic said at 9216 a guess, and a guess, Mr. President, cannot lead to reasonable doubt. Finally on this incident, the Prosecution submits that the purpose of firing a single round into the marketplace could only be to terrorise the civilian population. As expert witness Higgs said at 5030, and I quote: "Firing a single round into, as in the case here, a centre of a built-up area or a close to an area where civilians are known to be present would probably -- probably be more along the lines of to terrorise the population and to actually kill civilian casualties rather than any military objective." I now turn to the subject of modified air bombs, and again, I refer Your Honours to paragraphs 21 to 44 of the Prosecution closing brief. The Prosecution submits that it has proven beyond a reasonable doubt that the accused personally ordered the deployment of modified air bombs on Sarajevo throughout the amended indictment period in order to terrorise the civilian population. There is an abundance of credible evidence that the SRK developed, possessed, and used these notoriously inaccurate weapons, that in General Fraser's words had no legitimate military value during the conflict. And this evidence ranges from orders from the accused, them being P225 and P226, to witness testimony from UN witnesses and Bosnian police investigators. There is, on the other hand, no credible evidence that the ABiH possessed, let alone used, modified air bombs in the city against its own people. And for this reason the Prosecution submits that for all of its scheduled incidents involving modified air bombs the origin of fire was without doubt within SRK-controlled territory. Now of course during the trial there was evidence in respect of the TV tower incident and that is scheduled shelling incident 15 which occurred on the 28th of June, 1995. And the evidence, some of the evidence you have heard was that the ABiH fired this modified air bomb, but, Mr. President and Your Honours, the Prosecution submits that this evidence is not credible over and above the contemporaneous documentary and witness evidence proving that the SRK fired the modified air bomb at the TV tower --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Please slow down a little.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: -- including a document in which --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Please slow down.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. Including a document which the accused himself congratulates his troops on hitting the TV tower. And I now turn to this incident in some more detail. Mr. President, the Defence theory is that the modified air bomb was fired by the ABiH some 400 metres to the north of the TV tower in a built-up area near Mali Hum with no one noticing it except two UNMOs, Hansen and Knowles. You may recall during the testimony of expert Zecevic a video clip was shown demonstrating what a launch of an air bomb sounded like. Of course it is recalled that this launch was not of an air bomb in Sarajevo. However, it is instructive as to the sound such a launch would make. And the reason why I mention this is because it demonstrates, in the Prosecution's submission, the sheer improbability of such a weapon being fired from within the confrontation lines which the ABiH without it being noticed by anyone. Is it really possible that this is what happened, and if Hansen and Knowles are to be believed, only two UNMOs heard and noticed it and no one else did? The Prosecution submits that this is not at all possible. And not because of conjecture but because the positive direct evidence speaks to the absolute contrary. In cases before the Tribunal, if there exists contemporaneous recorded admission from an accused that a particular crime was committed then clearly this is the best evidence and this is what we have in this case. Your Honours, Prosecution Exhibit P42 is the infamous letter to all SRK troops from the accused on the state of affairs at the front, and in it the accused says the following: "Our artillery forces are responding with precision to the Muslim artillery attacks. In one such response on the 28th of June they hit had the BC/RTC/BH radio and television centre, the centre of media lies against the just struggle of the Serbian people." What better proof can there be regarding the origin of fire for this incident? Now, the Trial Chamber witness Knowles at T9395 did agree that it is theoretically possible that a commander may boast about things they never did to boost morale, but this was not the case here. In Prosecution Exhibit 629, a UN report of a meeting on the 9th of July, 1995, between an UNPROFOR officer and a Captain Novak Prodanovic from the Ilidza Brigade, the SRK captain is reported as having said that the SRK was firing Krema rockets at Sarajevo, including two at the TV building and I quote, "one of them hit it." Can an admission to UNPROFOR be a tactic to boost SRK morale? The Prosecution submits not, certainly not in addition to the accused's own admission as described above. However, if the Trial Chamber is minded to examine the testimony of Hansen and Knowles, then the Prosecution submits that their accounts are inconsistent and cannot raise reasonable doubt over the accused's responsibility. And again, Mr. President, this is in effect a summary of the Prosecution's written arguments found in paras 131 to 140 of its brief. Hansen does not explain why he waited day before he reported that the ABiH hit the TV tower when he had that alleged information on the day of the incident itself. Both Hansen and Knowles did not see the launch of the projectile and in fact Knowles had never seen the launch of a modified air bomb before. UNMO witness Brennskag however did see the launch and said it same from Ilidza under SRK control. Hansen testified that he was informed that the ABiH fired the projectile by another unnamed UNMO who he never identified. Yet Knowles testified that he saw the flight of the projectile with Hansen in the PTT parking lot. Who is correct here? Maybe this is why when Knowles was confronted with evidence that the UN had concluded that the SRK had fired at the TV tower through its protest letter to the accused and that --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Kindly slow down for the interpreters. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And that is P18 and the SRK admission on P42, Knowles conceded that it was possible that what he had seen was a secondary event by which he meant a second projectile. As Knowles said, "No one, including myself would wish to dispute the facts presented." Knowles agreed that it was a sudden, unexpected and very quick event and on all the facts the most reasonable explanation is that Knowles saw the same air bomb that Brennskag and W-156 did, the modified air bomb fired by the SRK that hit the TV tower. And further, Mr. President, the marks on the roof that W-138 testified about are consistent with the projectile flying from the west and not from the north in the area of Mali Hum. Lastly, the UNPROFOR commander General Smith testified that if the ABiH had been shown to have fired the round that hit the TV tower, it would have been brought to his attention. It was not brought to his attention. Mr. President, Your Honours, the Prosecution asks the Trial Chamber to arrive at the only available result based upon the evidence, and that is the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps launched this modified air bomb on the TV tower on the 28th of June, 1995, at around 9.20 in the morning, killing one person and wounding a further 28 civilians. I conclude. By proving beyond a reasonable doubt that the scheduled and unscheduled shelling incidents the Prosecution has established that General Dragomir Milosevic's responsibility -- has established his responsibility for the crime of terror, a violation of the laws and customs of war as charged in count 1 of the amended indictment,; the crime of murder, a crime against humanity as charged in count 5; the crime of inhumane acts, a crime against humanity as charged in count 6; and finally, the crime of unlawful attacks on civilians as charged in count 7 of the amended indictment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: That leaves out what?

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: It leaves out the counts related to sniping and those are my submissions, Mr. President and Your Honours. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. It seems fitting that I be the penultimate member of the Prosecution team to address you, Your Honours, because now after hearing the evidence of my colleagues I would suggest the terror count in this case is a charge that really captures the criminality of the accused, the criminality at issue, and it contextualises all the other evidence that you've heard my colleagues speak of, you've heard testimony about, and really brings home to all of us the sheer scale of the victimisation in this crime. The population of the city of Sarajevo, 250.000 people, were affected, terrorised. This wasn't an ethnic terror. These Serbs, Croats, and Muslims alike who lived in Bosnian government-held Sarajevo were terrorised, as Mr. Waespi said, not from the fear of being caught in a crossfire but because there was a battle nearby, what they suffered through was something very different than the fear that comes with war. They were the targets, Your Honours, of a politically motivated campaign of shelling and sniping that was initiated and ensured by the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps, maintained explicitly to terrorise its victims. These were attacks in which the accused took part at all levels, and they were effective. The civilians of Sarajevo did live in terror. Your Honours, it's the Prosecution's submission that there's no doubt that Dragomir Milosevic specifically intended and did send a clear message to the civilian population of BiH-held Sarajevo. They could never even hope for safety. The strength of the message was palpable because no one knew whether they might be the SRK's next victim. And I'm going to, in my submissions, highlight some of the evidence in that regard. You've heard abundant evidence from this trial as to the largely static nature of the front lines around Sarajevo throughout the siege and Sarajevo residents from within those lines, from all corners of the city from Bascarsija to Hrasnica from all walks of life, ages, ethnicities gave evidence to this Chamber as to the enduring violent nature of the campaign of shelling and sniping against them from SRK-held territory. They've given consistent, convincing evidence which shows that from August 1994 to November 1995 no civilian activity and no areas of BiH-held Sarajevo were safe from shelling or sniper fire. And that's because, as my colleagues have made plain, these attacks weren't aimed at neutralising any military targets. Quite the opposite. This wasn't conventional military activity at all as we've said. The intention was to ensure civilian casualties. Also, the trial record in this case is filled with evidence that throughout the period of this indictment shelling and sniping into BiH-held urban areas of Sarajevo wasn't justified by any military necessity. And there's not been any evidence that even one of the scheduled or unscheduled incidents you have put before you has realised a military advantage in favour of the SRK. Mothers walking with their children were shot by SRK snipers. Schoolchildren were shot. People riding trams in times of cease-fire were shot, and the evidence Your Honours have is that in all of those cases every single one of those victims were discernible as civilians. People were shelled and killed queuing to get their allotment of drinking water. They were killed shopping. They were skilled inside their own homes like in scheduled shelling incident number 6. Densely populated residential areas of Bosnian-held Sarajevo were shelled. Dobrinja, Novo Sarajevo. People who tried to rescue those who fell, even to investigate the origin of fire, were themselves shot at from SRK territory, and the people who lived within the lines, the people who remained in Sarajevo were forced to somehow adapt to their hostile environment.
