They lived in darkness like Witness W-35. They lived at night, like witness Sisic whose husband went out at night to find water so snipers wouldn't see them. They hid in basements and shelters. Going out to buy fresh fruit from a kiosk was a dream, but deciding whether or not you would let your child out to play was a reality. You never knew whether they would come back alive. All this is supported by, in our submission, neutral and experienced international observers, NATO generals, for example, who gave corroborative evidence to this effect. Further, all this evidence is corroborated by Mr. van der Weijden who said as my colleague Mr. Docherty made clear in no scheduled sniping incident to this indictment could the victim be identified as a combatant. And that's at P514, page 66. And by mortar expert Richard Higgs whose analysis for example, of SS 14 let him to the firm conclusion that this round that killed 7 and injured 12 was fired deliberately and aimed at the location -- at that location and fired at the particular time to cause maximum casualties. And that's at P589, pages 17 and 18. Your Honours have heard evidence of both the breadth and duration of the campaign. Mr. Waespi has already noted that by the time General Milosevic took office, it had been in place for more than two years. While the pattern and frequency of attacks fluctuated and we concede that, as Mr. Martin Bell told Your Honours that would largely be according to the seasons. They were relentless to the point where specific areas of Sarajevo became notorious as sources of sniper fire from SRK territory and where artillery and sniper positions could be identified as permanent, and in that regard I would point Your Honours to the evidence of General Karavelic. Your Honours, what I've just said only underscores evidence that in our submission leaves no doubt that a widespread, systematic campaign of shelling and sniping civilians in BiH-held parts of Sarajevo resulting in their death and injury was in place throughout the indictment period, and the nature, the manner, the timing, and the duration of these attacks of shelling and sniping are among the factors from which you can infer the general's specific intent to spread terror. And I'll move to discuss specific intent further later on in this presentation. But what I want to talk about now is whether the primary purpose of the campaign of sniping and shelling of civilians in BiH-held territory was to cause terror. To deal broadly with some defence positions that might go to the issue of primary purpose first, I'd just like to note that Defence has claimed we've all heard through this trial and in their brief that variously Bosnian Serb forces were not the aggressor, SRK forces wanted peace, that they were merely trying to defend their homes and what they perceived to be theirs or Bosnian Serb land. With respect to this point I would like to note that the territory in question around Sarajevo had been occupied and ethnically cleansed in 1992 to remain in 1994 under control of the SRK, and in that regard I would refer Your Honours to the testimony or to the report, rather, of Dr. Donia and the evidence of Mr. Harland. As to the desire for peace, Prosecution witness David Harland already explained that this desire for a cease-fire on the part of the Bosnian forces -- Bosnian Serb forces, was legitimate and importantly a reflection of the fact that by the indictment period having been militarily active in 1992 and 1993, they had already taken a little more than 70 per cent of the total territory of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, even more land than they ultimately sought to keep under a republic-wide peace agreement. Of course a cease-fire would have been of interest to the Bosnian Serbs to preserve the status quo and consolidate their dominant position throughout the country. But let's go back to Sarajevo. Even so, the evidence is that sniping and shelling into BiH-held Sarajevo continued through the indictment period and increased in its intensity as time went on. Defence has also repeatedly, and particularly for the year 1995, offered that SRK operations around Sarajevo were defensive and nothing more. A number of Defence witnesses almost exclusively SRK front-line trench soldiers gave evidence that their orders were not to fire at civilians. On this last point, Your Honours, whether the accused may have given such orders, the evidence is overwhelming, I would submit, even from Defence witnesses, for example, T39 who mentioned it and T22, that sniping and shelling of Bosnian-held Sarajevo from forces under the accused's control happened throughout the indictment period. It never stopped. And these assertions from Defence witnesses, as I've said, come from trench -- trench soldiers who confirm they have no personal knowledge of the situation within the Bosnian-held urban area of Sarajevo. In fact, one, Mr. Djukic, commented that he gave no credence to a siege of Sarajevo having been in place. Your Honours, on the other hand, we have coherent credible evidence from objective, third party observers of the situation within those BiH-held areas inside the city as well as the victims themselves who, time and again, say that sniping and shelling they observed and suffered had no discernible military objective. Its primary purpose, Your Honours, was specifically expressly to cause terror to the civilians, and the targets I've mentioned earlier speak for themselves, don't they? Mothers with their children walking, schoolchildren.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Are you going to tell us what terror is?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Would you like to hear comment about the elements, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Or do you think the term is self-explanatory? .

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I think the term is self-explanatory but I prefer to refer Your Honour, as I did when I spoke to you before during the 98 bis submissions, to the evidence of the people themselves. And in fact, it might be telling and appropriate at this moment to turn to one exhibit and the only exhibit I'm going to offer you, a clip from P612, which will come up in Sanction on your screen. This is a video, Your Honour, that Prosecution witness Martin Bell called one of the iconic images of the war, saying, "I think it conveys probably more than any single sniping incident the daily perils of the people in the city." If you could play that video, please, again. It's very brief.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: It speaks volumes, Your Honours. Those cowering people would be sprinting across the intersection to avoid sniper fire if it wasn't for that UNPROFOR APC. The people are like machines. There is no innocence in that image. There's no conversation. The innocence has been replaced by the unrelenting fear of being shot or shelled which was realised through the SRK's campaign of terror. And that, Your Honour, was defined by the Appeals Chamber in the Galic case as being acts or threats of violence, the primary purpose of which is to spread terror among the civilian population.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: That is a circle, isn't it? I said that's a circle.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: It's a circular definition. Terror is spreading terror.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: The terror -- the terror, in our submission, in my submission, is exactly what I've articulated to you immediately prior, Your Honours. No one knew whether they might be the next victim. It affected every waking moment of their lives. People for 15 months over the period of this indictment knew absolutely no sense of safety anywhere in the city. Terror is -- in this case, terror has been the intentional deprivation of a sense of security. It's been the primal fear that people feel when they see someone in front of them gunned down and that moment of panic when they try and run to help the victim, waiting for the next shots to come, and you've had ample evidence about that. Our brief contains a lengthy discussion of what terror means and the evidence of the witnesses in that regard -- excuse me, in that regard, and I would refer back to paragraphs 401 to 446 for an extensive, more extensive, discussion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I must say that I like your definition, Ms. Edgerton. Intentional deprivation of a sense of security and the primal fear that people feel when they see someone in front of them gunned down. That comes very close to it.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And I take that from the witness -- the witnesses and the evidence that's come before this Trial Chamber. I recall Martin Bell, who reported from Sarajevo at times throughout the conflict, characterising the only truly safe places in the whole city as the cave down by the Miljacka and the tunnels. How shocking that people in a European city would be reduced to seeking shelter underground for some measure of safety and security. And I quoted to Your Honours some months ago something that struck me from Mr. van der Weijden's evidence, and that was to deal with the feeling that you get under the eye of a sniper. He said, "The thought of never being safe affects everybody." And apart from being shot, the anxiety and it's obviously a pervasive anxiety, mainly comes from not knowing where or exactly when the sniper's going to strike. I think, Your Honours, Martin Bell's comments in respect of that clip that you saw were very telling. The constant attacks and the fear of those attacks demoralised civilians living in BiH-controlled territory. It exhausted them. It deprived them of hope. The victims actually tried to put words to it, and much weight comes to us from how they tried to articulate the sense of fear. Alma Cehajic Mulaosmanovic said that the suspense of whether you were going to be shot or not prevailed throughout the war and you will remember Ms. Cehajic Mulaosmanovic wasn't an elderly woman. She was a young woman whose testimony reflected that she had been affected by this pervasive fear and it hadn't left her by the time she came before Your Honours. W-35 said, "We were being shot at while going to get bread and water." She, too, was clearly bearing the marks of that pervasive fear. She talked of her perceptions of timing or pattern of attack. She said, and I quote from page 824 and 825: "Whenever there was a cease-fire or truce in Sarajevo, people would venture out to see sunshine, the earth. Children would go into parks and we who had families in other parts of town, we wanted to see our relatives, and that's when we suffered the most." For her a time of cease-fire or truce was a time where she might have felt some measure of safety to venture outside of her house, but look, that's exactly when they were victimised in her view the most. International witnesses apart from Mr. Bell echoed and elaborated on this from their perceptions. Mr. Brennskag said that he viewed the attacks on the civilians in Sarajevo as pure terror without military justification. General Sir Rupert Smith also elaborated on this saying he had no doubt the attacks on the civilians in Sarajevo, the campaign was essentially to terrorise, wear down the resolve of the defender, hold the presence of Serb pressure evidently in the minds of people on a daily basis and that was T3311. And Smith said the strategy worked particularly on the ordinary run of life within the city. So the fear pervaded in his view every aspect of the ordinary running of life. Mr. Bell, at 5264 of the transcript, said --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I have just a minute, please. Judge Mindua has a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [No interpretation]. [In English] No translation?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Yes, there is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: We have interpretation now. It's all right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was saying -- will you please excuse me, because it's just that I want to understand your definition of terror, and that's why I interrupted you. Could you please tell me, is terror a subjective feeling or an objective feeling? Is it the case that terror is an element of every war that takes place within an urban environment? What is your opinion? And I mean terror over civilians. Is it an inseparable element of every war within a city, a town? Is it the case that civilians are always in such circumstances terrorised?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your indulgence for a moment. I hope I -- I think I answer your question, Your Honour, and I hope I can answer you satisfactorily. Two things. In respect of the crime of terror, the actual affliction of terror isn't a requisite element of the offence. I should point that out. However, the Prosecution's position in this case is that it did very much occur among the civilians of Sarajevo at the hands of the SRK, and that has been established on the evidence beyond a reasonable doubt. That's the first thing. Second, as Mr. Waespi alluded to and I said at the beginning of my presentation, this terror, what the people of Sarajevo suffered through, is something very different from the fear that would normally accompany a war which could, Your Honour, be, for example, a fear that one might be struck by a stray bullet in a battle that was raging close by. Your Honour, when the drafters -- when the drafters of these provisions, I would submit, were crafting the wording for this offence, they meant to capture something very different and something that you very much find in Sarajevo, and that's why, Your Honours, they put the requirement of specific intent in that offence. They meant to capture the deliberate infliction of fear far and away apart from, completely not linked from any military objective or any military advantage to either of the opposing forces. And it's not just, as I said, the fear that comes from being nearby the combat. This is a fear calculated to demoralise, to disrupt, to take away any sense of security from a body of people who have nothing, Your Honours, to do with the combat. Has that answered to some measure your inquiry?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Just one further item of evidence with respect to the purpose, the object of this campaign, its primary purpose being one of the infliction of terror among the civilians of Sarajevo. Something which struck me was the evidence, again, of Mr. Harland who recounted the words of Bosnian Serb leader Radovan Karadzic talking about the Dobrinja-Butmir tunnel, in fact, which we've heard a great deal of evidence about, but Karadzic, Mr. Harland said, told him in respect to the tunnel, "You know, we could destroy it, but we're going to let the Muslims breathe." This for Mr. Harland was clearly strong evidence that confirmed to he and UN civil affairs the intention of Serb forces to terrorise the population of Sarajevo. Karadzic said, "We could destroy it." Harland confirmed that in his assessment they could have cut off all the food and water and actually forced the surrender of Sarajevo, but they chose not to. And that's at page at 375 of the transcript. And our submission, Your Honours, would be, in light of all you've heard absent any significant SRK offensive against the urban BiH-held area of Sarajevo during the indictment period, this is further evidence to support the conclusion that the intention of the campaign against Sarajevo was to terrorise its civilians. The shelling and sniping were meant to cause terror and they did so. My friends would have you believe, Your Honours, that the conditions and the character and the intensity of the campaign under Dragomir Milosevic's command eased somewhat from that of his predecessor General Galic, and in fact they make that assertion in their brief. But as Mr. Waespi pointed out under the tenure of the accused's command it became worse. And you've received evidence that the situation in Sarajevo came to resemble the earliest days of the war. Under the SRK and under Dragomir Milosevic things grew desperate. By 1995, the whole population of the city was exhausted and psychologically devastated. That comes from Mr. Overgard at T617. And if I may, Your Honours, I just need to ask that we go into closed session on two further occasions during my presentation to refer to the testimony of a protected witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Closed session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Private session, rather. Private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honours, it was in this context when people, civilians of Sarajevo were at their weakest in terms of the fear, the anxiety, the tensions that BiH-held Sarajevo was almost brought to, as we say in our brief, its knees. As my colleagues have said it was under the command of this accused that the SRK began to use weapons against the civilians of Sarajevo that hadn't been used before. Why are guided missiles, for example, which Mr. Harland understood should they be used in a real war to be used against tanks, were fired on apartment blocks? That's at transcript 452 to 453. P620 is a film of one of those missiles hitting the Presidency. It was in this context under the control and direction of Dragomir Milosevic that the rocket-propelled air bombs were added to the arsenal of instruments of terror and used against the city of Sarajevo. These were the weapons what Martin Bell colloquially described by their very nature as a weapon of mass destruction. "We might even call it a weapon of shock and awe," he said. "It's so destructive that it is more than most incapable of distinguishing between targets." And that's at 5262 of the transcript. And other witnesses also commented on the psychological impact for the people of Sarajevo to hear that these weapons existed. Fraser, Brigadier General Fraser said, "They sent shudders through everyone, including the UN." They -- and that, Your Honours is at pages 1825 to 1827 of the transcript. I was struck actually by the testimony of Dr. Zecevic, who also talked about the psychological, the intimidation impact of these weapons. At 4904 he said: "Can you imagine a person sitting in their apartment when a projectile hits and just blows off the top three floors of a building or a skyscraper? It's intimidating. Can you imagine that situation when the skyscraper was hit? From the psychological points of view it was indeed a formidable effect." In all of this, under the control at the time of the -- sorry, at the time, the SRK was under the control and direction of Dragomir Milosevic land routes into the city, into Sarajevo, were closed by Bosnian Serb forces. That was in March, as you've heard. In April the airport was also closed by Bosnian Serb forces, and with this the humanitarian airlift into the city which had been operational since 1992 ended for the rest of the war. Gas, water, and electricity were cut off. The bakery ran out of flour. In our submissions, Your Honours, this evidence that goes to show the level to which conditions in BiH-held Sarajevo deteriorated under the accused's command is some evidence that's very relevant to your considerations of whether he held the specific intent to spread terror among the civilian population. The Prosecution's submission is we've established that. Additional to everything I've said, the Prosecution has brought articulate evidence that during the period of this indictment in particular the terror campaign against the civilians of BiH-held Sarajevo was politically motivated. The pattern of terror through the attacks and humanitarian difficulty imposed on the civilians of Sarajevo was carefully modulated to serve as a form of pressure by Bosnian Serb forces to, among other things, extract concessions from the Bosnians at the negotiating table, and in that regard I would point to the evidence of Mr. Harland and Mr. Mohatarem by way of example; to stop attacks elsewhere in the battlefield in Bosnia and Herzegovina, even to deter a NATO military attack. In fact, Harland told the Tribunal that Serb leaders were explicit when they told him they would use their military apparatus to terrorise the population to get the political outcome they wanted. The Prosecution exhibit 1, page 27004, Harland said, "This was a common theme and they didn't even try to hide it from me." Pardon me, I cite to the wrong page. That's P1, 26953. The people of Sarajevo as we say in our brief, Your Honours, were bargaining chips, subject to the pressure of this campaign of terror to secure crudely some kind of concessions that would put the Bosnian Serb forces to advantage, and the Prosecution submits this also supports evidence or goes to the conclusion of the primary purpose of the campaign being to apply terror. If I could go -- ask -- if I could ask very briefly, Your Honours, for the last time to go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: The accused indeed implemented those orders, Your Honours, in the way he saw fit. And by the way, I should note that W-46 is corroborated by Brigadier General Fraser at 1818 when he said, "Within that little box called Sarajevo, General Milosevic was the guy in command." One of the ways as mentioned by my colleagues Dragomir Milosevic implemented those orders, exercised his command, was that he personally saw -- oversaw the deployment of air bombs against BiH-held Sarajevo, and the evidence in support of this that you've heard I think three of my colleagues refer to has actually come into these proceedings uncontested. So in our submission, Your Honour, this is incontrovertible evidence of his specific intent to cause terror among the civilian population of the BiH-held Sarajevo. The accused in our submission can't reasonably claim to be unaware of the potential for human casualties as a result of the use of the air bombs. Colonel Veljovic, their first Defence witness stated six SRK soldiers were killed testing the weapon, and that's at page 5801. Yet, on April 6, 1995, the accused issued the order my colleagues referred to as P226 directing an air bomb be launched at specific targets in Sarajevo where the greatest casualties and material damage would be inflicted, and the order was carried out. Scheduled shelling 6. Referring to a further incident mentioned by Mr. Sachdeva, the shelling of the radio and TV building, I would direct Your Honours to P42, which Mr. Sachdeva has dealt with in detail. There's no evidence before this Trial Chamber, Your Honours, to suggest that this letter, P42, represents anything other than a specific acknowledgement of SRK responsibility on the parts of Dragomir Milosevic for scheduled shelling 15, the air bomb attack on the TV building. Authenticity of that document has never been put at issue. Further, and again related to this incident, the SRK Ilidza Brigade liaison officer in P629, whose words are recorded in P629, described to a FreBat liaison officer the air bomb attack on the TV building, calling it psychological warfare aimed at upsetting the Bosnian soldiers engaged on the Treskavica front who would be worried about the safety of their families. And the Serb captain said because one of the rockets hit the TV building the journalists might have reported the incident and the BiH soldiers were informed about the existence of these weapons, and I quote, called terror.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: It has been suggested that the letter might have reflected nothing more than the kind of boast that one gets in military matters.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: In that regard, Your Honours, I would direct you to the testimony of - and I should choose my words carefully - W-156, who gave specific comments about this document and the authenticity of the document and the intention as he understood it from his own military experience of the speaker when he articulated those words. Further than that, Your Honours, would take the view that Mr. Sachdeva has adequately dealt with that question. I would actually suggest, Your Honour that, these documents emanating from the accused and recording statements of his staff are conclusive expression of the accused's specific intent to spread terror among the civilians of BiH-held Sarajevo, and any doubt Your Honours might have with regard to P629 is actually when looking in our trial brief, in our final brief, at the section on air bombs and the number, the quantity of orders issued by the accused and the quantity of air bombs dealt with in those orders that in fact that doubt that you might have about P629 is unnecessary, and you would find the document to be completely reliable. Your Honours, our submission would be that the accused knew about this campaign of terror against the civilians. He commanded it. He went, in P42, as far as to condone it. He was fully aware that the actions of his troops caused terror. And in that regard I would refer Your Honours to the notice and knowledge section of our closing brief. And in Dragomir Milosevic's command, he ensured the campaign continued. We talked about the definition of terror, Your Honours, and I opened with -- by pointing out that what happened to the civilians of Sarajevo was more than and distinct from the terror that comes with war. I would say, Your Honour, that that terror that they felt was the terror that came from knowing and believing, based on years-long, relentless, deliberate nature of the siege that they and their families and their children might be the next victims. And to close, Your Honours, just to remind you that no matter what argument of chaos or expressions of hopes and wishes for peace you might hear from my friends, to remind you of the testimony of Martin Bell who -- who also said that no matter what, it was the civilians inside the siege lines who bore the burden of the campaign of terror. And as for the SRK under the accused's command, I'd actually turn to Mr. Harland who said, "The application of instruments of terror against the civilian population, that was what the SRK basically did." And that's at page 325. Your Honour, it's our submission that terror was Dragomir Milosevic's primary purpose in laying the campaign of shelling and sniping against the civilians of Sarajevo. You have overwhelming evidence that this was actually his design. And I would close on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Actually I do have to ask leave, because I think we probably have exhausted already two hours allocated to us, but I still have a not-too-long section on the individual criminal responsibility of the accused and sentencing, and I hope to be done within 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, you may rest. You may begin tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but then I will ask for as much time, more, as the Prosecutor has taken.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. We always ensure equality. Yes, Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Of course the accused, General Milosevic, a professional JNA officer, was no stranger to the events that you heard about from my colleagues that unfolded in Sarajevo before he became the SRK commander in August 1994. The accused was involved in the siege from the outset, was in Sarajevo throughout the war in various important positions, most notably as General Galic's deputy and Chief of Staff. For the key role of a chief of staff, Your Honours, I would like to refer you to the testimony of Colonel Demurenko, page 7724, and Veljovic, pages 5831. I would also like to refer you to Prosecution Exhibit 738 in which the accused describes his role in Grbavica in 1992. The accused knew Sarajevo. He knew the front lines. He knew his troops. He knew the enemy. He knew the fate of the civilians inside the city. With this knowledge, Dragomir Milosevic became co-commander, inherited the campaign from his predecessor, did nothing to stop it or punish its perpetrators. In fact, he continued it for some 14 months. General Milosevic could and should have distanced himself from the previous commander. He could have said enough is enough. He could have made a difference. He did the opposite, Your Honours. He continued exactly along the same lines, introduced even a new dimension of terror. As you heard from my colleagues, the modified air bombs. The continuation of the campaign against the civilians of Sarajevo was undoubtedly expected from the accused by his superiors in Pale when they replaced General Galic. However, that does not remove anything from this accused's criminal responsibility. In this regard, Your Honours, let me add a comment about the relationship between the accused and his superior General Mladic. Of course the fact that the accused may have acted upon the orders of his superiors in Pale is, under Article 7(4) of our Statute, not a defence, although in theory it might give rise to mitigation. I will address sentencing in a moment but let me say this: A general in any army is a huge thing. It's the top of the tree. Generals have huge authority and commensurate responsibility. I cannot stress that more. There were only a handful of corps within the Bosnian Serb army and they were commanded by selected generals. The accused was one of them. Second, Your Honours, nobody is forced to become a general. There are enough candidates who want the general's rank. Also, Your Honours, look at the commanding, to use that word, personalities of the generals you have -- who have testified before you as witnesses. Third, we heard from a very senior UN official, and for that, Mr. President, we need briefly to go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: The fourth point about the relationship between General Milosevic and General Mladic is this: There is an incident in mid-1996 when the accused opposed General Mladic. Prosecution Exhibit 738 is a letter from the accused to General Mladic, and it carries the title "Inability to carry out orders, explanation." The accused confirms this letter that he has received on 16 May 1996 certain tasks from General Mladic and continues: "Having analysed them, I have concluded that I'm unable to carry them out." This shows that the accused could and did oppose his superior if he wanted. Fifth point, the accused certainly could and should not have ordered the use of air bombs. He could have done that based on Defence witness Veljovic, the first Defence witness's argument that the air bombs were a dangerous weapon and endangered the SRK troops, not the civilians, the SRK troops, an argument, I suggest that Mladic [Realtime transcript read in error "Mazowiecki"] should have been open to. Number six, the accused also could and should have investigated and punished just one SRK soldier for an attack on civilians. Seventh point --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi, there is some uncertainty about what is reflected in the transcript. You refer to Mr. Mazowiecki.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, that's an suggestion that General Mladic should have been open to, meaning the argument that air bombs should not be used because they would put SRK soldiers into a danger. General Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: We thought so. Thanks.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you for your observation. Seventh point. The accused could have resigned. I'm sure Mladic would have found a new commander in no time. Eighth point. There is absolutely nothing on the record, Mr. President, Your Honours, nor argued by the Defence, nor put to relevant Prosecution witnesses during cross-examination that there was any disagreement between Mladic and Milosevic as to how the campaign in Sarajevo should be fought or that the accused disagreed with the orders he received from the Main Staff. And the eighth point, an order to target civilians is patently illegal, see also P18 to which I will turn in a moment, and the accused have no duty whatsoever to obey such an order. In fact, he had, based on his own training in the military schools, and of course, based on the Geneva Conventions, no duty to implement that order. If the accused obeyed such an order, it is because he wanted it, as is demonstrated by his own orders targeting civilian areas, for instance, P226. Your Honours, it's the Prosecution's submission that General Milosevic had in theory and in practice all possibilities to make a difference to stop the senseless killing of civilians in Sarajevo. Your Honours, let me remind you of one of the key documents of the Prosecution's case, P18. I'm sure you remember it. Several witnesses testified about that. It's a personal letter. If it perhaps could be brought to the screen by e-court. P18. It's a personal letter of the acting UNPROFOR Sector Sarajevo Commander Robert Meille to the accused on the 30th June 1995. The letter addresses all the main issues related to individual criminal responsibility in this case. That's not the letter I was referring to. It's P, Prosecution Exhibit 18. The first issue, Your Honours and I'm sure you will remember this document. It's one page in English and B/C/S in original. It's notice to the accused of attacks on civilians. The second issue is the letter demonstrates the fact that repeated attacks on civilians in Sarajevo occurred. The third, it mentions the use and destructive potential of modified air bombs. Fourth, it reminds the accused of his obligations under Geneva Conventions. Fifth, it addresses the fact that the gunners were under the command and control of the accused. Sixth, it states that it was the accused who ordered the shelling. Seventh, it demands that the accused stop the bombardment. And finally eight, it even raises the possibility of an international court. There is not the slightest doubt, Mr. President, Your Honours, that the accused as the commander of the troops that lay siege on Sarajevo have effective command and control over these troops. Just one piece of evidence, Defence Exhibit D186, which is one of the first orders of the new SRK commander for full combat readiness to literally everybody around Sarajevo in August 1995. The fact that the accused had effective command and control is supported by every witness, international, local, the documents including also Defence witnesses and we have cited references in our closing brief. Ms. Edgerton already mentioned General Fraser's comment: "In the little box called Sarajevo, General Milosevic was the guy in command." It's also noteworthy, Ms. Edgerton mentioned it as well that, Defence did not dispute this fact. Of note, there is no mentioning in the entire trial record of any rogue elements, any snipers, uncontrolled gunners who might have fired into the city. Your Honours, an excellent way to see how the accused exercised command and control over his corps in Sarajevo, and indeed, how the SRK was organised and how it worked is to look at their own records. You will recall that OTP investigator Barry Hogan introduced to you almost a hundred SRK and VRS documents. It's P639, a spreadsheet outlining the relevancy of each of these documents. These SRK documents, I suggest, show a disciplined professional army in action. Let me just mention a few examples, aspects. Control over ammunition: P702 mentions that the commander, the accused Dragomir Milosevic, wants information on daily consumption of all types of ammunition and stating that unit commanders are personally responsible to General Milosevic for the implementation of the order. P666 is a very important document as it relates to sniping. Here Colonel Lugonja in August 1995, the SRK's assistant commander for security and intelligence states that sniping can only be stopped by orders from inside the corps. P663 talks about that key assets, inclusive air bombs and machine-guns are to be used throughout the SRK zone of responsibility as required and decided by the SRK commander. That's 15th June 1995, two weeks before the accused received the letter P18. We have mentioned other elements of command and control, the functioning of the SRK in our brief. I remind you of the excellent intelligence the SRK and ABiH had. You remember Witness Veljovic who testified about that, that they knew virtually anything that was happening inside the confrontation lines. See his evidence at 5850 to 51. Also, Mrkovic, another Defence witness at 8145, 46, and 8115. Look also at P698, 700, and 709. These are intelligence reports signed by Marko Lugonja, chief of intelligence and security of the SRK, showing how well-informed, again, the SRK was about the military targets, proper military targets inside the city of Sarajevo. These targets they could have, should have engaged and not the civilians. Finally, there was excellent work within the SRK staff. We heard had testimony from John Jordan, Colonel Dragicevic, Rupert Smith, again Mr. Veljovic at pages 5829 and 5841. And the last point under this section there were professional former JNA officers in the SRK. Mrkovic again at 8203 and 8209. Your Honours, let me go back to the specific role of the commander we heard from Defence witnesses the huge respect he had among them. This is a very important element for you to consider. There was strict discipline within the SRK, certainly as tight as under his predecessor General Galic. As an example, I refer you to the testimony of Veljovic again who said that on page 5837 the accused was "a real soldier, always in the front line, highly respected by the officers and soldiers alike." His orders were respected. He could order anything and he would have been obeyed. Your Honours, based on all you have heard today and what I just said all the elements of command and control, it's the Prosecution's case as we point out also in our brief on page 124, paragraph 454, that the overwhelming circumstances in this case lead to the conclusion that illegal acts on the civilians were ordered. Over 15 months in the context of an almost total siege of the city of Sarajevo a campaign of terror was conducted by a single but professionally organised and disciplined military corps under the command of General Milosevic, the accused. This campaign consistently and continuously targeted civilians directly and indiscriminately. The crimes were committed in a strikingly similar manner with hundreds of civilians killed and wounded. The attacks, you heard from Ms. Edgerton, increased or decreased in a calculated manner, often consistent with the political objectives of the Republika Srpska and the VRS at the time. These attacks were carried out by the SRK operating within a single operating chain of command functioning with military discipline. The SRK was under effective control of General Milosevic, who not only ordered indiscriminate weapons such as air bombs but failed to bring to halt to this campaign during the whole period he was the commander. This is despite the fact that he received protests and complaints. The only logical inference, Prosecution suggests, is that General Milosevic ordered the campaign of shelling and sniping of civilians with the primary purpose of terrorising. Let me very briefly address failure to punish. I will not go into this, as we call it, 7(3) evidence. We have discussed it in our brief and the record is very clear. The accused knew of the crimes and had all the necessary means at his disposal to sanction the behaviour of his subordinates. Colonel Dragicevic, and again, Veljovic at pages 5825, 5839 and 40, and also D - Defence Exhibit - 185 addressed all the means available to the accused, including the military police. P699 is a very concrete example of the exercise of authority of the accused to sanction a soldier to a prison sentence. In conclusion, there is ample evidence that as it relates to the crimes committed by SRK members against the civilian population of Sarajevo there were no investigations, let alone prosecutions, even though many other crimes such as threats, dereliction of documents or other kind of domestic violent crimes were investigated during this time period were effectively prosecuted. Let me finish, Mr. President, Your Honours, with sentencing. Article 24 of the Statute and Rule 101 and the developed ICTY jurisprudence, in particular Galic appeal judgement at paragraphs 391 to 456, provide the necessary guidance as to the factors involved. Of course, when assessing the gravity of the offence a Trial Chamber must take into account the inherent gravity of the crime, criminal conduct of the accused, the determination of which requires a consideration of the particular circumstances of the case and the crimes for which the accused was convicted, as well as form and degree of participation of the accused in those crimes. Let me very briefly address these factors. Inherent gravity of the crimes. The magnitude of the accused's crimes is enormous. If found guilty of count 1 of the indictment the accused will be held accountable for one of the most severe crimes that is or will ever be before this Tribunal, the crime of terror. In this case, the terrorisation of the population of Sarajevo. In addition, by participating in this terrorisation of the civilian population of Sarajevo, Milosevic is further guilty of crimes against humanity and violation of the laws or customs of war on a very large scale. The gravity of the offences committed by General Milosevic is established by their scale, pattern, and virtually continuous commission over many months. Hundreds of thousands inhabitants of Sarajevo, men, women, children and elderly persons, as you heard so graphically from my colleague Ms. Edgerton, were terrorised. Hundreds of civilians were killed, thousands wounded. You have already heard of the pattern of victimisation both in terms of scale and choice of victims. The particular cruelty of the crimes is shown by the fact that these acts were perpetrated against civilians in the perceived safety of their homes, at hospitals, schools, marketplaces and while commuting to the city or fetching water. General Milosevic is charged with a campaign of attacks against the civilian population of Sarajevo, which you heard it he inherited from General Galic. For the portion of the very same campaign carried out between September 1992, and August 1994, Your Honours, during which period General Milosevic was, of course, for over a year Chief of Staff to General Galic, General Galic was sentenced to a sentence of life imprisonment. Both the crimes charged in the indictment against this accused, General Milosevic, and his seniority and position within the SRK as commander make the case substantially similar to that against General Galic and so should be the applicable sentence. The accused's tenure as co-commander is shorter than of General Galic. However, what makes General Milosevic's responsibility even higher than that of General Galic is that unlike the former, General Milosevic personally oversaw and ordered for the first time during the siege in Sarajevo the deployment of modified air bombs, inherently inaccurate weapons with no legitimate military value even, and you heard it twice, the SRK refused to use these air bombs because they thought they were dangerous. Not for civilians, for their own soldiers. Form and degree of participation of the accused in those crimes, another factor. General Milosevic ordered the campaign of terror against the civilian population of Sarajevo as held by the Appeals Chamber in Semanza, I quote, "A higher sentence is likely to be imposed on a principal perpetrator vis-a-vis an accomplice, in that case of genocide, and on one who orders rather than merely aids and abets extermination." See also the Celebici Appeals Chamber who found that proof of active participation by a superior adds to the gravity of the superior's failure to prevent and punish and may therefore aggravate the sentence. Also, you heard it couple of times today, these were not crimes committed in the heat of a battle, Your Honours, or with little time to reflect on their consequences. Rather, these were continuing crimes in which the accused's mental and physical participation to their commission was renewed on a daily basis. Aggravating factors. An aggravating factor can be taken into account is the physical and psychological suffering inflicted on the victims. The actual infliction of terror, as you heard, is not a constitutive element of the crime of terror against a civilian population under Article 3 of the Statute as held by the Galic Trial Chamber. In this case; however, terror was actually inflicted on the civilians of Sarajevo, and such factor can be considered in aggravation of sentence. A second aggravating factor, Your Honours, is the accused's position of authority. General Milosevic was an experienced military officer who was 50 years of age at the time of his appointment as commander of the SRK. He had held various positions of authority throughout the conflict and was very familiar with the conflict in Sarajevo. General Milosevic was well aware of the extent of his obligations laid out in the military codes of the former JNA and then of the VRS. General Milosevic had a duty to uphold the laws or customs of war. The crimes that were committed by his troops would not have been committed without his assent. Despite being a professional soldier and career officer, General Milosevic not only made little effort to distinguish civilian from military objectives but willingly oversaw the targeting of civilians in Sarajevo. In his position of SRK corps commander, General Milosevic repeatedly breached his public duty from this very senior position, thereby abusing his position of authority. The accused's abuse of authority is a factor that aggravates his crime. In particular, rather than using his senior position as a professional officer to ensure that any military action was carried out lawfully, he gave orders to do the opposite. There are no circumstances that mitigate the culpability of the accused. In light of the above, Your Honours, only the imposition of a sentence of life imprisonment will adequately reflect the criminal liability of the accused. Thank you, Mr. President, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. I'll just give three decisions. The first relates to a motion filed on the 29th of September in which the Defence requested the removal from the record of Exhibit P546. The Prosecution notified the Trial Chamber that it has no objection to this. The Trial Chamber agrees with the parties that this document should not have been given an exhibit number and the request is therefore granted. The second motion is filed on the 8th of October. In that motion the Defence requests the admission of a document disclosed to it under Rule 68 on the 27th of September. The Prosecutor notified the Trial Chamber that it has no objection to the admission of the document. It also notes that the document pertains to meetings of UN personnel on the conduct of the Bosnian Serb and the Bosnian Muslims. The document is relevant and probative and it is admitted. The last is a motion filed on the 8th of October in which the Defence requests the admission of three statements pursuant to Rule 92 bis. The Trial Chamber has already decided on the admission of those statements. It did so on the 25th of July, 2007, holding that the statements were admitted upon fulfilment of the certification procedure set out in Rule 92 bis(B). This certification has now been fulfilled. The statements have thus already been admitted and the motion is therefore moot. We will adjourn until tomorrow at 2.15 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
